text_blocks.snippet: Social Security bankruptcy is a misnomer. While the Social Security trust funds are projected to be depleted in the coming years, this doesn't mean Social Security will cease to exist. It means that without changes, the system will only be able to pay out a portion of scheduled benefits from current tax revenue, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Bankruptcy, on the other hand, is a legal process for individuals or businesses to manage debt, and it doesn't directly affect Social Security eligibility or benefits.

list.snippet: The Social Security Administration (SSA) projects that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) trust fund will be depleted in 2033, and the combined OASI and Disability Insurance (DI) trust funds will be depleted in 2034, according to the Social Security Trustees.

This depletion doesn't mean Social Security will stop paying benefits entirely, but it does mean that the system will only be able to pay a portion of the scheduled benefits from the ongoing tax revenue, according to the Social Security Administration.

The SSA estimates that in 2035, they will still be able to pay 83% of scheduled benefits, and in 2098, they will be able to cover 73% of scheduled benefits from payroll taxes alone, according to captrust.

The Social Security Administration (.gov) reports that Social Security benefits may be reduced if the trust funds are depleted, but the system will continue to operate, paying out what it can from current tax revenue.
Bankruptcy does not affect your eligibility for Social Security benefits or the amount of benefits you receive, according to Experian.

However, Social Security income can be relevant in bankruptcy proceedings. If you file for bankruptcy, the court may consider your Social Security income when evaluating your ability to repay creditors.
If you commingle your Social Security funds with other income in a bank account, those combined funds could be at risk of being used to pay creditors in a bankruptcy case, according to AARP.
To protect your Social Security benefits in bankruptcy, it's recommended to keep them separate from other income in a dedicated account, according to AARP.
